summary:
I've been building an intranet dashboard — a fleet health monitor and app launcher for the ~29 internal and public services I run across a few boxes at home. It's a small Python service, but the interesting parts are the ones you only find by shipping it.

One is color. I'm red-green colorblind, so the usual green/amber/red status palette is close to useless to me — I actually ran a colorblindness simulation and measured the contrast in CIE-Lab: green-vs-red for "ok" vs "fail" scored a ΔE of 15.5, essentially indistinguishable, versus 98.1 for blue-vs-amber-vs-crimson. I also caught two counterintuitive traps that way: vermillion (a common "colorblind-safe" fail color) collides with amber under this vision, and pink desaturates toward gray and gets confused with "unknown." I locked the result in with a test that re-runs the simulation against the live stylesheet, so a future edit can't quietly reintroduce green as a signal color.

The other was a Linux permissions gotcha that took a while to run down. A hardened systemd unit (`NoNewPrivileges=true`) was silently returning zero cron jobs for one host while every other host reported fine — no error, just an empty list, which is the worst kind of bug. Turned out `NoNewPrivileges` disables the setgid bit that `crontab -l` depends on to read the spool directory. Fixed by adding the right supplementary groups to the unit. The debugging dead end worth remembering: transient `systemd-run` probes looked like proof the sandbox was broken, but they were actually failing to start at all — testing against the real unit was the only way to see the actual problem.

I also picked up a DNS surprise while wiring up CI for it: an internal hostname I'd been using turned out to be a real, publicly registered domain. My local network only overrides the IPv4 record, so IPv6 quietly resolves to the public internet — meaning a client that preferred IPv6 could push credentials off my network without any error. Nothing's broken today because IPv4 wins in practice, but it's a reminder to actually check where a name resolves before trusting it, not just assume the override caught everything.
